OPS03-BP02 Test and validate any and all changes
Test every change before it reaches production, including
    application code, infrastructure, configuration, security controls,
    and operational procedures. When you run tests immediately after
    each change, defects are cheap to fix and developers get fast
    feedback.
Desired outcome:
Your changes are tested before they are delivered, and your
        pipeline blocks any change that fails.
Your developers see test results quickly and act on them without
        leaving their workflow.
Your testing covers application code, infrastructure,
        configuration, and security controls, not code alone.
Every artifact meets your shared testing standard before it is
        promoted.
Common anti-patterns:
Teams deploy a change with no tests, and it fails in production
        and causes an incident.
Teams deploy new security group rules without testing them, and
        the change makes the application unreachable for customers.
Developers modify a method that has no unit test, and the defect
        surfaces only after release.
Testing happens manually at the end of the process, so feedback
        arrives too late to be cheap to act on.
Benefits of establishing this best
    practice:
Change failure rate drops because defects are caught before
        release.
Software quality improves as tests document expected behavior
        and guard against regression.
Developers gain confidence in their changes through fast,
        automated feedback.
Security and compliance controls roll out with evidence that
        they work as intended.
Infrastructure changes such as scaling policy updates are
        validated before they affect live traffic.
Level of risk exposed if this best practice
    is not established:
High
Implementation guidance
The earlier a test runs, the cheaper the defect is to fix, because
      less work has been built on top of it.
Unit tests check a single function in isolation and run in
      milliseconds. Integration and end-to-end tests exercise components
      together and take longer. Static analysis and software composition
      analysis (SCA) inspect code and dependencies for known
      vulnerabilities without running the software. Weight your test
      suite toward fast, narrow tests and use slower, broad tests
      sparingly. A suite that takes an hour to run gets skipped under
      deadline pressure.
Test infrastructure definitions, configuration, security controls,
      and operational procedures the same way you test code. Code tests
      never catch security group rules that block legitimate traffic, a
      scaling policy that fails under load, or a runbook that no longer
      matches reality. Treat every artifact that can change production
      behavior as something to test.
Automated tests remove manual effort and human error, and give
      developers fast feedback. Automate everything repetitive, and
      reserve human judgment for work such as exploratory testing,
      usability review, or security assessment of a novel design.
      Publish results to developers immediately. Agree on a testing
      standard with stakeholders that defines which tests every artifact
      must pass and who is notified when they complete.
Use
Kiro
to write code
      artifacts, find and resolve bugs, and develop unit tests across
      large codebases.
AWS CodeBuild
runs tests on each artifact, and
AWS CodePipeline
sequences those tests into gates a change must
      clear before promotion. The
AWS Deployment Pipeline Reference Architecture
catalogs the
      test types you can place at each stage.
Implementation steps
Define a testing standard with your
            stakeholders:
Agree on which tests every artifact
            must pass, the compliance and governance requirements to
            cover, and who is notified when tests complete. Use the
AWS Deployment Pipeline Reference Architecture
as an
            authoritative list of test types to include.
Instrument artifacts with automated
            tests:
Add the tests your standard requires so
            they run as part of the integration pipeline, and keep each
            suite within a predictable duration, such as under ten
            minutes. Use
Kiro
to generate
            unit tests with boundary conditions and to find defects.
Run tests automatically in the
            pipeline:
Configure
AWS CodeBuild
to run your tests on each change, and use
AWS CodePipeline
to order them into gates that block
            promotion on failure.
Test infrastructure and security
            changes the same way:
Validate infrastructure
            definitions, configuration, and security controls in a
            pre-production environment before they reach production.
            Apply the same automated gates to these artifacts that you
            apply to application code.
Publish results and store validated
            artifacts:
Send test outcomes to developers as
            each gate passes, so feedback is immediate. Promote only
            artifacts that clear every gate, and store them in an
            artifact repository for deployment.
